hook: Before the world knew Bob Marley, he worked the night shift in Delaware.
beats: In 1966 he moved in with his mother in Wilmington, Delaware.
Under the name “Donald Marley,” he worked at a DuPont lab and a Chrysler plant.
He was saving money to start his own record label back in Jamaica.
Years later, that time is often linked to his 1976 song “Night Shift.”
payoff: Wilmington now has a One Love Park across from the house where he lived.
question: What job were you doing while chasing your dream?

hook: Fela Kuti's parents sent him to London to become a doctor.
beats: It was 1958. He was 19, and the plan was medical school.
Instead, he enrolled at Trinity College of Music.
In London he formed Koola Lobitos, mixing jazz with highlife.
Back in Africa, that mix grew into a sound he named Afrobeat.
payoff: London later put a blue plaque on the house where he lived as a student.
question: Did you ever take a path your family didn't plan for you?

hook: The most famous part of “Ain't No Sunshine” was never supposed to be there.
beats: Bill Withers wrote it while making toilets for Boeing 747s.
He was 31, still working in the factory.
In the middle he sang “I know” 26 times as a placeholder for lyrics he hadn't written.
The other musicians told him to leave it. So he did.
payoff: The placeholder became the moment everybody waits for.
question: What's your favorite Bill Withers song?

hook: Her own country took away her citizenship. The world gave her nine passports.
beats: In 1960, South Africa revoked Miriam Makeba's passport. She couldn't go home for her mother's funeral.
In 1963 she spoke against apartheid at the United Nations.
South Africa responded by stripping her citizenship.
Countries including Guinea and Ghana issued her passports.
payoff: She held nine passports and honorary citizenship in ten countries.
question: Which Makeba song should every young person hear?

hook: Reggae got its name from one song.
beats: In 1968, the Maytals released “Do the Reggay.”
It was the first popular song to use the word.
Toots said it came from street slang for a scruffy look.
The name stuck to the new sound coming out of Jamaica.
payoff: The Oxford English Dictionary credits Toots and the Maytals in the word's history.
question: Name a reggae song that never gets old.

hook: In 1951, about 25,000 people paid to watch a gospel star get married.
beats: Sister Rosetta Tharpe married her manager at Griffith Stadium in Washington, D.C.
Her backup singers were the bridesmaids.
After the vows, she played a concert in her wedding dress.
Decca even released a record of the ceremony.
payoff: Many call her the godmother of rock and roll.
question: Who's the most underrated pioneer in music history?

hook: A Grammy-winning guitarist went home and became mayor.
beats: Ali Farka Touré of Mali was called the father of African desert blues.
He always returned to his hometown, Niafunké, and to farming.
In 2004 he became the town's mayor.
He used his own money to grade roads and power a generator for electricity.
payoff: Music took him around the world. He brought it back home.
question: What would you build in your hometown if you could?

hook: Nina Simone dreamed of being a classical pianist. One school said no.
beats: In 1951 she auditioned for the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia.
She was rejected. She always believed it was because she was Black.
She started singing in an Atlantic City bar to make a living.
That's where Eunice Waymon became Nina Simone.
payoff: In 2003, Curtis gave her an honorary degree. She died two days later.
question: Which Nina Simone song stops you in your tracks?

hook: Louis Armstrong once mailed a trumpet to a youth band in South Africa.
beats: Teenage Hugh Masekela asked a priest, Trevor Huddleston, for a trumpet.
Huddleston got him one, and other kids asked for instruments too.
They became the Huddleston Jazz Band.
When Huddleston met Armstrong, he told him about the band. Armstrong sent a trumpet.
payoff: Masekela grew into one of South Africa's greatest musicians.
question: Who gave you your first push in music?

hook: Hip hop started at a party to buy back-to-school clothes.
beats: August 11, 1973: Cindy Campbell rented the rec room at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx.
Her brother Clive, born in Jamaica, played the music.
He brought Jamaica's sound system culture with him.
As DJ Kool Herc, he stretched the drum breaks so people could dance longer.
payoff: That night is widely seen as the birth of hip hop.
question: Reggae and hip hop: what's the best song that connects them?

hook: The father of Ethio-jazz was supposed to study aeronautical engineering.
beats: Mulatu Astatke left Ethiopia to study, but music pulled him in.
He trained in London, then became Berklee College of Music's first African student.
He blended Ethiopian scales with jazz and Latin rhythms.
He called the sound Ethio-jazz.
payoff: In 2012, Berklee gave him an honorary doctorate.
question: Have you heard Ethio-jazz? Drop a favorite below.

hook: She became a world star at 47, singing barefoot.
beats: Cesária Évora sang in the bars of Mindelo, Cape Verde, from age 16.
For decades, almost no one outside the islands knew her.
In 1988, a producer brought her to Paris to record.
The album was called “La Diva aux pieds nus”: the barefoot diva.
payoff: She went on to win a Grammy and take morna to the world.
question: Is it ever too late to be discovered? Tell us a story.
